title: The Fragrance of Job's Integrity
english: Today the athlete of the inhabited world has come to us. He has come to us as a stranger and a combatant of equal honor to the angels, he who is much struck by the devil and much testified to by God; he who is much beaten by the devil and much receives rewards from the watching angels; he who is much scourged by the Enemy and has been raised up by God as a great crown-bearer for the world.

For thus, conversing with himself, he was saying: 'It seems to me that I have been used for you in another way, rather than so that you might appear righteous?' Who then is able to praise such a one worthily? Who will dare to weave rewards worthy of his manliness? Who will attempt to ascend to an infinite sea of praises? For just as no one possessing understanding would ever dare to cross the expanse of the sea with human steps, so no one of the wise and great teachers will ever attempt to relate to the listeners the praises worthy of that courage and of the triple-layered soul. For all human wisdom his achievements surpass; all crown-bearing his contests surpass.

Do we not receive an angelic tongue, so that, having touched with our fingertips, so to speak, that jar of myrrh, we might all at once fill the assembly? For only if we attempt to touch the vessel of Job and shake it a little, immediately the assembly is filled with the fragrance of the myrrh. Let us then hear the history being told concerning him: In all these things happening to him, Job did not sin with his lips against the Lord. Did you see the testimony that was rousing the praise of the angels? Did you see the testimony that was shaming the devil with his attempts? In all these things happening to him, he did not sin. This is the [testimony] of God...

It is a testimony before the whole church, like a precious myrrh, that brings joy to those who hear it. Oh, the precious vessel kept in one place in Arabia, its fragrance spreading through the whole inhabited world! Oh, the vessel, struck by myriads of stones, wounds, and arrows from the devil, yet not pouring out the myrrh! Great toil was exerted by the blow, so that the vessel might be crushed and the myrrh of piety might be vanished; and through the stench of the wounds, it strove to dim the fragrance of the myrrh.

For even his body escaped the pulling of the wounds; but the vessel remained being wounded, and the myrrh was not lost, so that we might also say to him with confidence: 'Name to you, having been emptied, myrrh.' It is necessary, therefore, to raise up the athlete naked, as he was before, so that seeing that wonderful image, we may be strengthened by the nature of things: that God, wishing to show the devil that He has righteous men on the earth—no longer deceived by flattery according to Adam, but crowned through myriads of torments and scourges—continued this drama to happen.

'Depart, you great-minded ones,' he says, 'who, having deceived Adam and flattered the woman, cast out [man] from paradise; behold, a man living divided by the commands of Scripture, and having through intellect established the unwritten law of nature. Bring forward myriads of insults, myriads of flatteries, myriads of torments, if you are able to shake this best soul.' Behold, you cast the first man out of paradise. See now, attempt, if you can, even to trip the athlete from his feet by hardship.

But, if it seems good, let us run back a little upward into this history: There was a certain man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job. And that man was blameless, righteous, God-fearing, true, abstaining from every evil thing. Such was also Adam before...

title: The Devil's Strategy and the Unshakable Athlete
english: Regarding being persuaded by the woman. Because of this, that one was not persuaded by the woman, so that he would not become like him. That one, clothed in incorruptibility, as he who formed him knew, and so that he might be persuaded by the woman, became naked and was judged. This one was naked and was not persuaded by the woman, and so that he might not be persuaded by the woman, he put on the crown-bearing of the angels.

That one, so that he might be persuaded by the woman, fell from the delight of paradise, and made the mother earth a place of thorns, and inherited death; this one, so that he might not be persuaded by the woman, took freedom from toil and from plagues, and inherited the kingdom of the heavens. That one, defending himself to God, was saying: 'The woman whom you gave to me, she gave to me, and I ate.' Oh, what a defense lacking in forgiveness! She said, 'Eat'; I said, 'Do not eat.' Why then did you listen to the woman and fail to listen to God? But the blessed Job was not so.

But how? After striking back, he said: 'You have spoken like one of the foolish women.' There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job. Why did he name the land Uz? Because of you, so that you might learn that the fellowship of sinners is not able to make the righteous sin, but the choice of the pious must have a stable and firm opinion. For this is the land of Arabia, a dwelling place of weary and corrupted men. All were lawless, all were God-hating, all were unstable, all were proud, and descendants of Isaiah, and bearing many sins; but such a sea of impiety was not able to extinguish the shining one of piety; such a land of evils was not able to stifle the beautiful breath of endurance.

Therefore, the devil attempted to approach him. Why? Because he saw him becoming rich through alms rather than through money. Listen to him saying truthfully: 'I was an eye to the blind, and a leg to the lame'; and again, 'I wept for the helpless, and sighed seeing a man in necessity.' And not only through words, but also through works he was exceedingly rich, a whole treasure of goodness being found for those in need. For what does he say elsewhere? 'I did not go out from my house begging with an empty womb; the mouth of the widow blessed me; and from the fleece of my sheep my shoulders were warmed.'

Thus it is clear that a complete treasure flows through all things: through words, through works, through alms, through the protection of the penitent, and through the assistance of those who pray. But observe what the devil does: he first snatches away all that previously belonged to him, and lastly he takes the children. He took first the herds of camels, he took the flocks of sheep, the great number of donkeys, and the largest herd of oxen; he removed everything, and lastly the children.

Why? Pay attention then with all precision: first he took all his possessions, then the children; he took the hereditary things, and then he destroyed the heirs, so that he might strike him in every way, even through the children. First he began to make existence vanish; first he began to snatch the hereditary things while the heirs were still living, so that while the sons and daughters were standing, he might take advantage of the loss of the properties to strike the righteous man with despondency. For the evil demon aims lest, with the children having been lost beforehand, he should even come to the realization of the loss of the properties.

But the truly unyielding and brave athlete—he who is much struck and yet is crowned through all things, he who receives many arrows and through those very arrows pierces the devil, he who, being armed on both right and left with the weapons of righteousness, does not grow weary, does not weep, and is not shaken—he neither was bent by the loss of the properties, nor did he allow the death of the children to plunder his piety. Instead, he remained like an unshakeable tower, being uprooted from below upon the earth and yet being established, and secured even unto the heavenly heights.

A first angel came and says to Job: The pairs of oxen were plowing, and the raiders came and plundered them, and they killed the servants with swords. While this one was speaking, another angel came and says to Job: Fire fell from heaven and burned up your sheep, and the shepherds were likewise consumed. Look what the devil does. For because he saw him standing bravely in the first and second plague, and not at all shaken from his tribulations, fighting and not flinching, he devises some device...

title: The Deception of the Messenger
english: To do such a thing: fire is cast from the air, so that it might seem that fire is being sent from heaven, and so that he, thinking that God is fighting him from the heavens, might blaspheme God, fighting Him unjustly through such a division. He says, 'Fire fell from heaven and consumed your sheep and your shepherds.' While he was still speaking this, another angel came and said to Job: 'The horsemen made three heads for us, and they surrounded the camels and captured them, and they killed the boys with swords.'

But even in all these things the blessed Job remained, like an unshakable pillar, like an unmoving tower, like an undefeated combatant, unbending and unyielding, rather attacking than being attacked. For when someone is weary from being lowly, fighting much and benefiting nothing, fighting much and not at all prevailing, he himself is rather the one receiving the lashes for his vain labors. While he was still speaking this, another angel came.

The war is continuous, but in vain for the one suffering; the arrows are more frequent, but the rewards are more splendid. He does not allow him even to breathe for a moment, so that he might not reason something wise according to the innate piety of the wrestling match. He sent all the arrows, and he did not defeat the athlete; he emptied his quiver, but he was not emptied of his endurance. Let the lawless be shamed for nothing.

Since then he himself turned away humbled and crushed, having wrestled much and having been defeated through all things. For he sent [strikes] against the shepherds, against the herdsmen, against the sheep, against the camels, against the sons, against the daughters, against the household, against the body, through friends, through servants, through worms, through wounds, through sores. He emptied everything, and did not break his piety. He breached the wall, but did not empty the treasure.

Whatever swords the tyrant of the inhabited world moved, through fire, through swords, through earth, through captivity, through blood; he pierced everything, and made the athlete rather more courageous. For this reason also the prophet cried out saying: 'The swords of the Enemy have run out to an end.' Perhaps also he says to him: 'It is hard for you to strike against thorns.' He took all the money, the possessions...

And who is this last messenger? 'While your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking in the house of their elder brother, suddenly a spirit came from the desert, and it struck the four corners of the house, and the house fell upon your children, and they died.' And so that you may know, beloved, that it was not a man who was discussing these things to Job, but the devil himself, disguised in the form of a man; learn this with all precision: 'While your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking at the side of their elder brother, suddenly a spirit came from the desert, and it struck the four corners of the house, and the house fell upon your children, and they died.'

How do you know, tell me, that it came from the desert and struck the four corners of the house? You are a man, and how did you see the spirit? With what eyes did you behold it? And how did the spirit strike the four corners of the house? If you are a man, and you were inside the house, then surely the house also encompassed you; but if you were outside, how were you seeing the things happening within? If you are a spirit, show who you are; do not disguise yourself in the form of a man.

He says: 'Of your sons and your daughters eating and drinking at the side of their elder brother.' See how the blessed Job was filled with all understanding and wisdom, and how he was securing the friendship of the children. For he reasoned that since Cain and Abel were two brothers, being the only ones in the inhabited world, they had no occasion for war; for all the earth lay commonly under the authority of both. And thus, envying the honor of Abel, Cain rose up and murdered his brother.

Because of this, the blessed Job offered sacrifices to God concerning the unknown every day, countering the first [impulse], and saying: 'May my children never conceive evil in their hearts toward God.' And concerning the things happening to them, whether in word or in contention, he made them eat with one another every day, remembering that even if they should have some pettiness toward one another, the table and the arrangement of the bread make them be transformed into friendship, and cast out the malice that was approaching, knowing that through the...

title: Job's endurance and the greatness of the narrative
english: The table of continuous life is released to them by the hardships that fall upon them. But the slanderous devil, in such a time, sought to destroy the children who had committed no sin. In the hour of midday, when all were united and joining together for peace, he sent the unmerciful war against them. They were practicing friendship, but he wielded a sword; they were building up love, but he was destroying the house. At that very hour, the house became a tomb, the table a vessel of calamity, the shipwreck a pastoral fold, and everything became full of beasts.

What then is that brave man? He was not broken, and he did not fall. How shall I praise him? What word will be sufficient? What toil will be enough for such a narrative? O brave and blessed soul! O, you who do not possess an excess of great endurance! Truly, beloved, my soul is poured out and my conscience is disturbed, even as I see Job being crowned. But I am more poured out in soul now, seeing the crowned one, whereas he then saw the calamity of the children before his eyes. I am poured out in soul, and I think you are likewise divided.

How then shall I speak this great tragedy, even while bearing the diadem of encomiums upon my tongue? Parents according to the flesh, when they have a son following them with his last breaths, sit around; they listen to his last words, they clasp his hands, they arrange instructions concerning the deceased, they kiss the mouth, the last affections of the fathers. Then the boy has given up the soul, as the one who gave command instructed; the parents shape the body, stretch out the hands, close the eyes, straighten the head, stretch out the feet, wash him, clothe him in worthy burial garments, and console themselves regarding their own calamity.

But what is this compared to this brave athlete? He departed into the house which was at once the same and one, and at the same hour a house and a tomb, a banquet and a grave, a feast and mourning becoming. He searched and sought the limbs of the children, and found wine and blood, bread and a hand, an eye and dust. At times he took a hand, at times a foot, and at other times he lifted up a head along with the earth, and the stones, and the timbers; and at times a part of the belly, and at other times of the...

The internal organs were being scattered along with the flesh. That sky-reaching combatant sat, looking upon the limbs of the children, which were torn apart. He sat having joined limb to limb, hand to arm, head to chest, and knees to thighs. For the calamity was not merely one of the occurrences, but a destruction surpassing all reason, arising from diabolical activity and tyranny. Thus Job sat, the truly patient and unyielding, the blessed one, distinguishing the limbs of his children, lest he should mix the limbs of the females with the males, or the male form should be joined to the female limbs. O brave soul, surpassing even the praise of the angels! Why? Because in all these things happening to him, Job committed no sin against the Lord; rather, instead of all these, he offered a complete thanksgiving to God instead of a sacrifice, saying: 'Blessed be the name of the Lord, now and always, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.'

To the righteous and blessed Job, Discourse 4. 1. Great matters require great narrations, and the brilliant histories of the righteous require a brilliant tongue and intellect; the intellect sincerely contemplating the divine Scriptures, and the tongue boldly interpreting the divine. I speak especially regarding the present subject, that is, of those who labored for the blessed Job, which things, passing through all that walks under heaven, turn away the reason of his endurance. Moreover, even if the argument of the subject conquers our weakness, I know well that the grace of God provides the argument, not because of the worth of the speaker, but because of the embassy of the Fathers.

But let us come to the narration: There was a certain man in the land of Ausitis. It is necessary first to observe what power the preface possesses, and for whose sake the historian has fashioned the preface, 'There was a certain man.' Since he was about to narrate a virtuous life, greatly surpassing our own condition, he had to show the nature in advance so that no one, looking upon the excess of the struggles, might think it to be a foreign nature and not a human one. Thus, you might marvel at the intention: that being a man, he lived more excellently than a man, having shared a common nature with all,

title: The Contrast of Lineages
english: He has brought the soul up higher than the world. There was a certain man in the land of Ausitis. He preaches him from his nature, and he preaches him from the land, so that just as having heard of him as a man, you marvel that he lived as one above a man, so if you learn also about the land from which so much fruit blossomed, you will truly marvel at what kind of rose has grown in the midst of thorns. Pay attention precisely.

The land, therefore, of the Ausitis, was the land of Esau; for the Ausitis was from Esau. And he names the land of the profane and evil Esau, as the Apostle says: 'Is there not a harlot or a profane man, like Esau?'—so that you may marvel from what educations of wickedness such a fruit of truth has blossomed. But not only did the land of Esau bring him forth, but also the root of Esau was himself; for he was a descendant of the slanderer. For the Scripture says that Job was the fifth from Abraham. And how fifth, listen: Abraham begat Isaac, Isaac [begat] Esau, Esau [begat] Raguel, Raguel [begat] Zarrah, Zarrah [begat] Job. He therefore had the succession coming down from Abraham through Esau to him. Thus he shows the root, so that you may marvel at the fruit.

And who was Esau? A harlot and a profane man. And who was Job? The one from the harlot, this same venerable and marvelous man, the one now set before us for narration, the one saying: 'If my eye had followed a woman not mine own, would my wife be pleased with another man?' Esau had much mixture of women, being insatiable toward debauchery; but Job had the law of life in his manner, and he abstained so much that he did not seek out the beauty of strangers; and from fornication and adultery he abstained so much that he did not even attend to the women not yet betrothed, that is, the unremembered virgins; for it is necessary to use a more explicit expression. He abstained so much from attacking foreign marriages that even toward the unremembered virgin, for whom there was no danger, he did not incline his eye before...

Regarding unchastity. And who is witnessing these things? Job himself. He says, 'A covenant was distributed to my eyes, and I did not understand it in my youth.' See to what extent the things of piety reached him through discipline. He trains the eye toward piety, and he trains the limbs toward righteousness; and though bearing the succession from fornication, he shone out with the greatest self-control.

Esau was a brother-slayer in intention; for even if the deed did not come to pass, the intention is accused. For it is said that Esau said in his heart, 'Let the days of my father's mourning approach, and I will rise up against Jacob my brother.' The root, therefore, is brother-slaying; but he who blossomed from the root is the champion of righteousness. That one waged war by nature and regarded his brother as a stranger; but this one regarded strangers as brothers, saying, 'I became to the orphans as a father, and instead of a husband to their mother. A justice which I did not know, I searched out, and I stopped the unrighteous.' And he who carries the succession from Esau appropriates all foreign things, by setting foreign things as his own.

Esau reckoned in his mind to kill Jacob; but Job offered sacrifices for his sons, thinking, 'Lest they have sinned in thought.' Because that one had planned murder in thought, this great and brave athlete, fearing that these too might receive the venom of sin in thought, offered a sacrifice and one calf for sins. For Job said, 'Perhaps my sons have thought evil toward God?' Consider the precision to which the discipline of character reached him. And what does he do? Since Esau and Jacob, the ancestors, were at war with one another—not because Jacob agreed to evil, but because Esau began toward evil—he dissolves the disagreement of the ancestors by the table. He makes his sons feast with one another every day, so that the habitual table might dissolve the venom of evil.

title: The distinction between blamelessness and faultlessness
english: The children of Job loved one another, being trained in concord from their youth, practicing peace and being educated in harmony, eating and drinking together. He says that they also took the three sisters to eat and drink with them. What is the benefit of this to the listener? And why did he add the sisters to the fellowship? It was so that it might be shown to what extent temperance governed their banquet, and that it was not a riotous and spilled laughter, nor an intemperance insulting the table; for this reason he introduces the well-mannered virgins, to show that the occasion of the banquet was not being insulted by drunkenness, but was being crowned by harmony.

There was a certain man in the land of Ausiti: a dove among hawks, a sheep among wolves, a star among the clouds, a cypress among thorns, the plant of righteousness in the village of unrighteousness. And that man was blameless.

Pay close attention. Those from the outside set the definition: 'What is man?' 'Man is,' he says, 'a rational, mortal animal.' Such are the definitions the philosophers desire; but the Scripture does not give such definitions, but rather what? A blameless, righteous, true man. If anyone asks you and demands a definition, 'What is man?' say to him, 'Blameless, righteous, true, abstaining from every evil thing'; for as one has not been testified to regarding such accomplishments, no man exists. For if he possesses the character of nature, but insults it with the wickedness of his will, he hears from the prophet: 'Being a man in honor, he did not understand; he was cast down with the mindless cattle, and was made like them.' And that man was blameless.

The praise is not small. Test the word so that you may marvel at the intention. An accusation is one thing, and a reproach is another; for an accusation is brought against the heaviest of sins, but a reproach occurs regarding the lightest of faults. Therefore the writer wished to show that the righteous man was not only far from accusations, but also from reproaches. No one called him out as one who had done great things, just as no one reproached him as one who had done small things. This is a great proof: that he, whose life was in the middle, was beyond reproach. For if you do not have an accusation to bring concerning adultery or murder, such a man is beyond reproach; but with a reproach, you bring insult, slander, or invective.

Such a person is outside of blame, yet he flees from reproach as if from a drunken stupor. He wished to show that he was far from even the smallest of stings, saying: He was blameless, righteous, truthful, and God-fearing, abstaining from every evil thing. Therefore, God, intending to show Abraham that the first thing in virtue is the blameless, says to him: You are well-pleasing before me, and become blameless. The term 'blameless' is understood as an extremity of manner.

But the apostle Paul, since he had among the Gentiles those drawn away from polytheism, those gathered from wickedness, and those gathered from fornication and adultery, did not add the extremity of virtue. Rather, as he came into the inhabited world filled with fornication and adultery, he wished also to establish shepherds for the world, since at that time the beautiful things of virtue were scarce, appointing bishops, saying to Titus: Appoint bishops, as I commanded you, if anyone is faultless. 'Blameless' had no place then, since, as I said, the peak of piety was scarce. Blamelessness is great, but faultlessness is the middle; and [blamelessness] is great among evils, while the good is small.

For this reason he said: A man of one woman. Not because this is now observed in the Church—for the priest must be crowned with perfect purity and holiness—but because then, in regard to those in fornication, the matter was great, he says: Appoint bishops, as I commanded you, if anyone is faultless, a man of one woman; not because he laid down this law, but because he recognized the plan. For he knew that when the word of piety is blooming, nature itself will possess the good as a pleasant thing, and the selection will be of the better ones.

Blameless, righteous. Therefore, it is not possible to become righteous without having first become blameless. Truthful. What does the truthful man intend? He who does not shape his appearance differently from his actual state, who does not shape himself in temperance while being clothed in intemperance, who does not show justice in outward form while bearing injustice in the heart. This man is truthful, and immediately God-fearing. For when there is blamelessness, when there is righteousness, and when there is truth, then true God-fearingness is composed. Abstaining from every evil thing. Since many abstain from many sins, but they do not abstain from all...

title: Participation in Christ through the Saints
english: He says that he intends to set forth the peak of virtue: abstaining from every evil thing. Therefore David also says: those who love the Lord, hate evils. For it is not possible to be both God-fearing and to do evil.

And he sets forth his very existence, because he had seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred nomad donkeys. Why does he set these forth? Not so that you may marvel at Job's wealth, but leaving to you, the listener, the abundance of his being, so that, when you see him after this having been stripped of his possessions and not complaining, you may marvel that, being deprived of so many good things, he does not reject the benefactor, nor insult the Creator. These things, therefore, were written, not so that you may marvel at wealth, but so that you may praise the endurance and the patience of the righteous, and always have the fear of God before your eyes. But the sequence of the argument will be stored up for another time.

For the devil, brothers, since he saw him prospering with this temporary wealth, and by this temporary wealth storing up eternal wealth, reasoned that just as righteousness was entwined with him while he was prospering, so also poverty and virtue will be entwined with him while he is impoverishing. Therefore he tries to strip him of material things, so that he may strip him of his advantages.

Here, then, let those who say precisely: 'Was not Job rich? Was not Abraham rich? Why then do you propose poverty to us?' pay attention. I will say also to you: become rich according to Job, and I pray that you may acquire more; become according to Abraham, and all the earth will be joined to you for wealth. Say also you, as Job: 'My door is opened to everyone afflicted'; say, 'I warmed the shoulders of the poor'; say, 'From the fleece of my sheep the shoulders of the poor were warmed'; say, 'And the mouth of the widow blessed me'; and get rich with the wealth that you desire. For wealth will be found not for yourself, but for the poor, being managed. For my door, he says, is opened to everyone afflicted.

Imitate the extremity of this love of the poor; clothe yourself with the zeal of endurance; be manly against the adversaries; think of equal things. But these things are only to this extent. May it happen to us, having zeal and endurance at home, to have also the sequence of the lacking...

He remains, demanding from us those things which are lacking, and making us follow the sequence of the contemplations. May it happen to us through knowledge to fulfill the feast, and having shared in the sufferings of the saints, to share also in the passion of Christ. For truly, brothers, the sufferings of the saints preceded the passion of Christ justly. For the sufferings of the righteous preceded like lightning bolts, so that after these things Christ might appear, as Paul says, the one suffering with all and being glorified with all.

Therefore, having followed the prayers and supplications of the holy Fathers, and having followed what has been spoken, and having expected the things that are lacking, let us send up glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, unto the ages of ages. Amen. To the righteous and blessed Job, Word 3. 1. Bring it forth, so that we might also grasp the premise, and you the listening; and let us all become acquainted with the evening sequence of Job, and with faith let us present ourselves to the word of endurance.

For it is incongruous that Job, sitting upon misery, should not grow numb toward piety, while we, dancing in the church, should be hesitant toward the truth; and that he, being surrounded by myriad wailings of his own misfortune, should not have his soul overthrown, while we, wandering through hymns and spiritual songs and divine Scriptures, should surrender our readiness with laziness. Job, the body being eaten away by worms, preserved the soul unharmed toward piety; worms did not overcome him, so shall those who have strengthened us overcome us? Let us also become men, men according to the measure that is pre-allotted.

For the man is characterized by the blameless, the righteous, the true, and the God-fearing. And just as by common custom, when someone sends his own servant or son on some deed, he is encouraged, saying: 'As a man, grasp this deed,' and he makes the common name his own wonder; even if all are called men, only he is a true man, the one preserving the image and not making the prototype beauty vanish. He called him a man, so that from the common nature you might praise the intention. He called him from the land of Ausitis, so that from the land of the [unclear] you might praise the fruit of impiety. His possessions said to him, so that...
